summary:
SPACECORE is a free web tool that turns NASA’s SPHEREx archive into something anyone can explore. A user types an object name or sky coordinates, and the page gathers every SPHEREx image of that region, aligns them, combines each six-month visit into one cleaner frame, and plays them as a blink animation, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out against the fixed stars. 

users can switch among the six detectors, compare or subtract two epochs to reveal motion, and get an on-the-fly spectrum from SPHEREx’s 102 infrared bands. An Aladin sky view adds Gaia and WISE catalogs, and every search can be shared or embedded with a URL. Results are cached, so the five test targets, including Barnard’s Star, WISE 0855 and R Draconis, load in under a second even if the archive is down.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, but its data lives in large files built for specialists. SPACECORE lets students, teachers and amateur astronomers search for fast-moving stars, brown dwarfs or even a hidden Planet X themselves.
details:
What it does and how it works

SPACECORE is a free web tool for exploring NASA’s SPHEREx data. A user types an object name (or coordinates in decimal or h:m:s format) and the tool:

  1. Converts the name into sky coordinates. For fast-moving stars it corrects for their motion across the sky, so the target stays centered.
  2. Asks NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive for every SPHEREx image that covers that point, across all six detectors.
  3. Groups the images into epochs, one for each six-month visit of the telescope.
  4. Downloads small cutouts in parallel, re-projects them onto a common north-up grid (6.15″ per pixel) and combines each epoch with a median. This removes cosmic rays and noise.
  5. Shows the epochs as a blink animation, a before/after slider, a difference image (what moved or changed brightness) or a sum.
  6. Builds an on-the-fly spectrum: each exposure sees a different infrared color, so the tool measures the star’s brightness in every image (aperture photometry with background subtraction, in mJy) and plots it against wavelength from 0.75 to 5 µm. The aperture follows the star’s proper motion, and saturated points are marked.

An Aladin sky view adds Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogs for context.

Benefits

Nothing to install, a bilingual interface (English/Spanish), and every search can be shared or embedded with a URL. The server does the heavy work, so it runs on any browser. Results are cached, so the five test targets load in under a second even when the NASA archive is down.

Expected impact

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, but its data comes in large files built for specialists. SPACECORE opens it to students, teachers and amateur astronomers, so anyone can hunt for nearby moving stars, brown dwarfs or a hidden Planet X, and researchers can quickly check candidates before downloading full data.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, Astropy, Astroquery/PyVO (IRSA SIA), reproject, NumPy, Pillow, httpx.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, Vite, HTML Canvas, Plotly, Aladin Lite.
  • Infrastructure: Docker and Docker Compose, Redis cache (Upstash in production), Google Cloud Run, Vercel, GitHub.
  • Data: SPHEREx spectral images (IRSA), Gaia DR3, AllWISE, DSS2.
  • AI assistants: Claude Code and Codex.

Creativity

We brought back the blink comparator, the same technique Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto in 1930, and applied it to a 102-color infrared survey. We also turned SPHEREx’s design into a feature: since every pixel sees a different wavelength, hundreds of ordinary images add up to a spectrum.

Factors our team considered

  • Reliability: the archive often returns errors, so we added retries, limited parallel downloads and precomputed results.
  • Scientific honesty: saturated stars are flagged, and the photometry is labeled as approximate.
  • Accessibility and cost: Spanish and English, free-tier cloud services.
  • Reproducibility: the whole system runs with one Docker command.
